lessons.title: Binary Search Concept
lessons.concept: Binary search is an efficient algorithm to find a target value in a sorted array by repeatedly dividing the search interval in half. It compares the target with the middle element and discards one half of the remaining elements each step.
lessons.formula: Precondition: array sorted. Steps: low=0, high=n-1; while low<=high compute mid=(low+high)//2; if arr[mid]==target return mid; if arr[mid]<target low=mid+1 else high=mid-1.
lessons.worked_example: Array [1,3,5,7,9], target 7: mid=5 -> 5<7 so search right half [7,9], mid=7 -> found.
mistakes: Applying binary search on an unsorted array
Updating boundaries incorrectly (infinite loop or missed element)
Off-by-one errors in loop condition or mid updates

lessons.title: Iterative and Recursive Approaches
lessons.concept: Binary search can be implemented iteratively using a loop or recursively by calling the function on the selected half. Both follow the same divide-and-conquer logic; iterative form avoids recursion overhead and call stack usage.
lessons.formula: Iterative: while low<=high adjust bounds. Recursive: base case low>high return -1; else compare mid and recurse on left/right half.
lessons.worked_example: Recursive search for 3 in [1,3,5,7]: mid is 3 -> return index. If searching 6, mid 3 < 6 search [5,7], mid 5 < 6 search [7], mid 7 > 6 search empty -> not found.
mistakes: Missing base case in recursive implementation
Passing incorrect low/high bounds in recursive calls
Assuming recursion is always faster (it has call overhead)

lessons.title: Complexity and Use Cases
lessons.concept: Binary search reduces the search space by half each step, giving logarithmic time complexity. It is ideal for lookups in sorted arrays/lists and for problems involving monotonic conditions (binary search on answer).
lessons.formula: Time: O(log n). Space: O(1) iterative, O(log n) recursive (call stack).
lessons.worked_example: In an array of 1024 sorted elements, binary search needs at most about 10 comparisons (since 2^10 = 1024) in the worst case.
mistakes: Confusing binary search O(log n) with linear search O(n)
Forgetting sort precondition cost if data is unsorted
Using it where random access is inefficient (e.g., linked list without indexing)

practice.question: Binary search works correctly on which type of array?

options.C: Only arrays with unique elements but unsorted

practice.explanation: Binary search relies on ordering to discard half the elements after each comparison, so the array must be sorted (by the search key/order).

practice.question: In binary search, if arr[mid] is less than the target, what should be done next (ascending sorted array)?

options.A: Search left half by setting high = mid - 1
options.B: Search right half by setting low = mid + 1

practice.explanation: If the middle element is smaller than the target in an ascending array, the target can only be in the right half, so set low = mid + 1.

practice.question: What is the auxiliary space complexity of an iterative binary search?
practice.explanation: Iterative binary search uses a constant amount of extra space for variables like low, high, and mid, so auxiliary space is O(1).

practice.question: For array [2, 4, 6, 8, 10] (0-based), searching for 8: first mid index is (0+4)//2 = 2 (value 6). What is the next search range?
practice.explanation: 6 < 8, so search the right half by moving low to mid+1 = 3. New range is indices 3 to 4 ([8,10]).

questions.question: Which condition is typically used in an iterative binary search loop (when low and high are inclusive bounds)?
questions.explanation: With inclusive bounds, the search continues while there is at least one element in range, i.e., low <= high. Using low < high can miss the case where low == high.

questions.question: Binary search on 1,000,000 sorted elements takes at most about how many comparisons (order of magnitude)?
questions.explanation: Binary search is O(log2 n). log2(1,000,000) is about 20 comparisons in the worst case.

questions.question: In a recursive binary search, what happens when low becomes greater than high?

options.B: The search continues on the right half
options.C: The target is not found (base case)

questions.explanation: If low > high, the search interval is empty, meaning the target does not exist in the array; this is the not-found base case.

questions.question: Why is binary search generally not efficient for a singly linked list (even if sorted)?

options.B: Finding the middle element requires traversal, losing random access benefit
options.C: Binary search only works on numbers

questions.explanation: Binary search needs efficient access to the middle element. In a singly linked list, reaching mid requires O(n) traversal, making overall performance poor compared to arrays.

questions.question: For sorted array [1, 2, 4, 4, 5, 7], standard binary search is primarily designed to:

options.A: Always return the first occurrence of a duplicate target
options.B: Find an index of the target if present (occurrence not specified by basic form)

questions.explanation: Basic binary search checks equality at mid and returns that index when found; it does not guarantee first/last occurrence for duplicates without modification.
